## Easy explanation
Think of an A/B test like a bakery offering free samples of two slightly different cookie recipes to alternating customers entering the shop, counting which tray empties faster before deciding which recipe to bake in commercial quantities.

## Details
In digital product experimentation, incoming traffic is split randomly between Version A (the control baseline) and Version B (the experimental variant containing a targeted change, such as a redesigned call-to-action or altered pricing layout). Behavioral metrics—such as click-through rate, signup rate, or revenue per visitor—are tracked across both groups. By utilizing statistical hypothesis testing, product teams verify whether observed performance lifts represent genuine causal impact rather than random variance.

## Technical definition
A randomized controlled experiment in software optimization wherein two or more variants of a user interface or algorithmic flow are evaluated concurrently to establish statistical superiority.

## Examples
An online hotel platform tests a green booking button (Variant B) against its existing blue button (Control A), discovering that the green variant produces a statistically significant 4.2% increase in reservations.

## Easy explanation
Think of acceptance criteria as an inspection checklist before buying a house: the front door lock must work, hot water must run within five seconds, and windows must latch tightly; if any item fails, the key is not handed over.

## Details
Acceptance criteria remove guesswork by setting explicit boundaries for what is in and out of scope for a given work item. They are established collaboratively during backlog grooming or sprint planning before code is drafted. Teams frequently adopt scenario-based formulations such as "Given [context], When [action], Then [expected result]" to clarify user journeys. Quality assurance engineers directly transform these criteria into functional test suites.

## Technical definition
The formal stipulations and functional preconditions that a software deliverable must verify to satisfy the business requirements of the product owner.

## Examples
For a password reset feature: "Given a registered email, when the user requests a reset, then a single-use token valid for 15 minutes is dispatched via email."

## Easy explanation
Accrual accounting records sales the moment goods are handed over, and records bills the moment services are received, even if the actual bank transfer happens weeks later.

## Details
Contrasting with cash-basis bookkeeping, the accrual approach matches expenses directly against the revenues they helped generate during the same reporting period. This requires creating receivables for delivered orders awaiting payment and payables for incurred supplier costs, giving an accurate operational representation of ongoing enterprise profitability.

## Technical definition
The accounting convention mandating that transactions and economic events are recognized when performance obligations are met or obligations incurred rather than when cash is transferred.

## Examples
An IT consulting firm performs software audits in November and bills the client $30,000; it recognizes the $30,000 revenue in November even though client payment arrives in January.

## Easy explanation
If a sensor serves as the eyes and ears of an automated system, an actuator serves as its muscles: it receives instructions from a controller and executes a tangible physical movement, such as spinning a motor, opening a valve, or sliding a deadbolt.

## Details
Actuators translate low-energy electrical or algorithmic instructions into mechanical work. Depending on the energy medium utilized, actuators are categorized into electromechanical (stepper motors, solenoids, servos), pneumatic (compressed air pistons), and hydraulic (pressurized fluid cylinders). Key engineering metrics include stroke length, torque, slew speed, positioning accuracy, and holding force. Closed-loop control systems often integrate feedback sensors with actuators to verify that the commanded mechanical position is accurately achieved.

## Technical definition
A mechanical or electro-mechanical device that accepts an input control signal and transforms stored energy into controlled physical motion, torque, or mechanical displacement.

## Examples
A motorized ball valve actuator that rotates ninety degrees to shut off the water supply when an automated leak detector triggers an alarm.

## Easy explanation
If an electronic neon sign flashes an advertisement five separate times while you stand waiting at a bus stop, you have personally generated five impressions for that ad.

## Details
An impression represents the atomic unit of digital ad delivery. It increments whenever an ad server transmits a creative asset to a publisher's webpage or mobile application and renders it within the browser DOM. Crucially, impressions count gross volume rather than net audience: if one individual refreshes a web page four times, the ad server logs four distinct impressions. Industry standards differentiate served impressions (the asset was downloaded) from viewable impressions (at least 50% of the creative was visible in the active viewport for at least one continuous second).

## Technical definition
A single instance of an advertising creative element being retrieved from a content delivery network and successfully painted within the client device screen viewport.

## Examples
A promoted post on a social media news feed passes through a user's screen in the morning and appears again in their feed during the evening commute, registering two impressions from that single user.

## Easy explanation
Unlike a simple calculator that answers only when prompted, an agent acts like an autonomous administrative assistant: you give it a goal, and it looks up schedules, books flight tickets, checks hotel reviews, and handles follow-ups on its own.

## Details
An AI agent couples a foundation model core with external affordances: planning mechanisms, memory modules, and tool interfaces (APIs, web browsers, bash environments). Driven by an agentic loop, it perceives environmental feedback, deliberates on next actions, invokes functions, and assesses whether intermediate milestones satisfy the overarching goal before yielding a final status.

## Technical definition
An autonomous decision-making computational entity that processes state observations, formulates action sequences via policy inference, and executes tool calls to attain designated objectives.

## Examples
A coding assistant agent reading an error log from a continuous integration runner, locating the offending source file, writing a unit test, patching the bug, and verifying the fix.

## Easy explanation
Just as standardized tests like the SAT or IELTS provide a uniform ruler to compare students from different schools, an AI benchmark gives all models the exact same exam questions under identical testing conditions.

## Details
Benchmarks establish reproducible performance baselines across algorithms and hardware platforms. In computational engineering, suites like MLPerf measure operational metrics including inference latency, tokens-per-second throughput, and power draw under defined service-level agreements. In model capabilities, benchmarks assess specific domains such as mathematical reasoning, coding proficiency, multi-turn dialogue, or multimodal perception using fixed test partitions and scoring rules.

## Technical definition
A standardized reference workload, test dataset, and measurement methodology designed to quantitatively assess and compare algorithmic capabilities or computing system efficiency.

## Examples
An engineering team evaluating two cloud server architectures by executing the standardized MLPerf Inference suite to compare token throughput per dollar.

## Easy explanation
An anonymous source is like a whistleblower slipping a folder under a door: they provide crucial facts while their real name stays strictly hidden.

## Details
Investigative journalism depends on confidential informants to expose corruption, corporate malfeasance, or security failures when coming forward openly would bring retaliation. Editors mandate strict standards before granting anonymity: the information must be vital to the public interest, unobtainable on the record, and independently verified by secondary sources or physical documents. Reporters protect source identities even when facing subpoenas or imprisonment.

## Technical definition
An individual who provides confidential testimony or documentation to a journalist under a binding agreement that their identity will remain undisclosed in published reports.

## Examples
A senior municipal auditor secretly shares financial ledgers with an investigative journalist, allowing the paper to document public procurement fraud while citing only a confidential official.

## Easy explanation
Think of a waiter in a restaurant: you review the menu, give your order to the waiter, the kitchen prepares it, and the waiter brings the meal back without you ever having to enter the kitchen.

## Details
An API exposes specific endpoints that accept requests formatted in standard protocols such as HTTP, WebSockets, or gRPC. It hides the underlying internal business logic, database schemas, and implementation complexities while enforcing security, rate limiting, and authentication tokens.

## Technical definition
A formally specified interface contract establishing data structures, operation signatures, and protocol constraints through which independent software entities interact programmatically.

## Examples
A ride-hailing app sends GPS coordinates to Google Maps via an HTTP REST endpoint to display an interactive map route.

## Easy explanation
Like an office building where each department has a specific room number: you go to room 101 for customer support and room 202 for billing.

## Details
Endpoints combine a host domain, a URL path, and an HTTP method. When a client makes a network request to an endpoint, backend routing tables inspect the path and execute the corresponding controller function to process the payload and formulate a response.

## Technical definition
A targeted communication gateway represented as a uniform resource locator (URL) that receives remote method invocations and returns structured digital resources.

## Examples
Pointing a payment checkout webhook to `https://api.example.com/v1/payments/charge` using an HTTP POST method.

## Easy explanation
Like a receptionist in a sprawling corporate headquarters who checks visitors badges, answers basic inquiries, and directs each visitor to the correct department elevator.

## Details
An API gateway sits between client devices (mobile apps, web browsers, external partners) and downstream microservices. Instead of clients maintaining dozens of independent remote endpoints, they call a unified gateway domain. The gateway intercepts calls to enforce JSON Web Token authentication, rate limiting, request validation, payload transformation, and circuit breaking. It can also aggregate multiple downstream responses into one unified JSON payload, reducing client radio power consumption on mobile networks.

## Technical definition
An architectural component providing centralized edge routing, protocol translation, authorization enforcement, and telemetry aggregation across microservice topologies.

## Examples
A financial platform gateway receiving 12,000 inbound requests per second, verifying customer authentication tokens, and fanning out parallel calls to account balances and transaction histories.

## Easy explanation
Aspect ratio is like the shape of a picture frame: whether it is a square, a wide cinema rectangle, or a tall vertical postcard, the ratio tells you how broad the view is compared to its height.

## Details
Expressed as two numbers separated by a colon, aspect ratios dictate composition in photography, cinema, television, and web development. Traditional analog television adopted 4:3, modern digital high-definition standards standardized on 16:9, and widescreen cinema commonly shoots in 2.39:1 anamorphic format. The explosion of mobile social video introduced vertical 9:16 framing, forcing production houses to plan safe framing areas that accommodate multi-platform cropping.

## Technical definition
The mathematical ratio of the width to the height of a rectangular display area, sensor capture frame, or digital graphic asset.

## Examples
A video editor configures project sequence settings to 16:9 widescreen (1920x1080 pixels) for YouTube broadcast while creating a secondary 9:16 vertical crop (1080x1920 pixels) for mobile story distribution.

## Easy explanation
An asset is anything valuable that a business owns or controls—like cash, equipment, delivery vans, or software patents—that helps it generate money.

## Details
Assets appear on the left or top of the balance sheet and are split between current items convertible to cash within twelve months, and non-current items like machinery and real estate. Under modern accounting frameworks, an item qualifies as an asset only if the business exercises control over it and can reliably quantify expected inflows of economic utility.

## Technical definition
A resource controlled by the enterprise as a consequence of past transactions from which probable future economic benefits are anticipated to flow.

## Examples
A distribution depot controls $500,000 in warehouse racking, $200,000 in electric delivery vans, and $150,000 in customer invoices due next month.

## Easy explanation
When reading a legal contract and seeing the word "it," your attention immediately jumps back to the specific company name mentioned earlier so you comprehend what "it" refers to.

## Details
Attention computes relevance scores across tokens using Query, Key, and Value representations. The dot product between a query vector and all key vectors measures pairwise affinity, scaled to prevent saturation, and normalized through softmax into a probability distribution. The final output is a weighted sum over value vectors. Self-attention enables tokens within the same passage to contextualize each other regardless of distance.

## Technical definition
A dynamic pooling function that computes a weighted sum of value vectors according to similarity coefficients derived from query and key vector dot products.

## Examples
A translation network processing the pronoun "she" in a medical narrative and focusing attention weight heavily on "the surgeon" established in a prior sentence.

## Easy explanation
If an announcement is read aloud in an auditorium containing one hundred people, your reach is one hundred: repeating the announcement three times raises the impression count to three hundred, but your reach remains exactly one hundred people.

## Details
In digital advertising and social media analytics, reach measures the net audience size of unique individuals exposed to a campaign, eliminating duplications from repeat views. Measuring reach accurately presents technical challenges because modern consumers interact across multiple devices including mobile smartphones, tablets, work laptops, and connected televisions. Platforms deploy statistical deduplication models, unified login identifiers, and privacy-preserving identity graphs to map multiple device impressions to a single unique person. Advertisers balance reach against frequency: maximizing reach expands top-of-funnel brand awareness, whereas increasing frequency drives message retention.

## Technical definition
A media measurement metric representing the deduplicated aggregate count of unique authenticated profiles or statistically estimated distinct human observers within a target demographic exposed at least once to an ad delivery event.

## Examples
A smartphone company runs a product launch teaser on social video feeds that accumulates five million total impressions, but deduplicated audience analysis confirms that the video actually reached two million distinct individuals.

## Easy explanation
Like a highway toll plaza: when rush hour arrives and lines grow long, the station opens additional toll booths automatically, closing them down when evening traffic thins out.

## Details
Autoscaling monitors health metrics such as average CPU utilization, memory pressure, or incoming request rates. When thresholds are breached, the scaling controller launches additional instances or pods and registers them with the load balancer. Once traffic drops, it gracefully drains connections and terminates excess nodes to minimize cloud costs.

## Technical definition
A feedback-driven control loop that dynamically adjusts workload instance capacity in response to observed telemetry metrics against defined threshold policies.

## Examples
An online ticketing cluster configured to maintain 5 server instances at baseline, expanding automatically to 35 instances when concert tickets go on sale.

## Easy explanation
B-roll is like the background b-side of a cassette: while the speaker talks about growing coffee beans, the video shows close-ups of harvesting red coffee cherries rather than staring at their talking face the entire time.

## Details
In video production and broadcast journalism, A-roll captures the primary talking head or central subject, while B-roll provides cutaway shots. Video editors drop B-roll footage onto timeline overlay tracks to mask jump cuts when trimming speech pauses or stumbles. Cinematographers intentionally shoot varied establishing shots, medium details, and extreme close-ups on location to give post-production editors ample visual rhythm options.

## Technical definition
Auxiliary visual footage captured to complement, cover, and contextualize primary narrative cinematography or interview sequences during editorial montage.

## Examples
In a documentary profile of an oceanographer, the editor cuts away from the seated interview to sweeping aerial drone footage of research vessels navigating arctic ice shelves.

## Easy explanation
Imagine academic research papers: whenever other scholars cite your published work as a helpful reference in their own bibliographies, your reputation among academic peers grows stronger.

## Details
Backlinks constitute one of the fundamental signals in search engine ranking algorithms, historically pioneered by Google's PageRank. When reputable and topically relevant domains link to a page, crawlers interpret the connection as a signal of trust and authority. Webmasters can qualify outgoing links using HTML `rel` attributes, distinguishing organic editorial endorsements from paid partnerships (`rel="sponsored"`) or user-contributed forum posts (`rel="ugc"`). Low-quality, reciprocal link farms or manipulative link schemes violate search policies and can lead to algorithmic devaluation.

## Technical definition
An inbound hyperlink embedded within a foreign origin document utilizing standard anchor markup pointing toward a destination uniform resource identifier on an independent host domain.

## Examples
A cybersecurity blog publishes a research breakdown of a zero-day exploit, and major technology news outlets link to the original article as their primary citation, boosting the author's domain visibility.

## Easy explanation
Like a kitchen sink drain: if you turn the water faucet on at maximum blast and the pipe below drains slowly, the basin overflows onto the floor unless you turn down the faucet handle to match the drain rate.

## Details
In asynchronous processing pipelines, fast data producers (such as high-speed network sockets) can easily outpace downstream consumers (such as slow disk writes or database inserts). Uncontrolled buffering leads to OutOfMemory crashes or massive latency queues. Backpressure introduces a feedback loop: downstream consumers signal their capacity upstream using credit tokens, pull-based requests, or rate throttling. If consumer buffers fill, upstream publishers pause or drop low-priority records until downstream capacity recovers.

## Technical definition
A feedback flow-control protocol in asynchronous communication topologies that prevents memory exhaustion by coupling consumer capacity to producer emission rates.

## Examples
A video encoding pipeline where a downstream transcoding worker requests batches of 5 raw frames at a time from a camera ingest stream, ensuring memory buffers never overflow during compute-heavy frames.

## Easy explanation
Think of a balance sheet as a financial selfie taken on a single date, showing every item the business owns alongside every dollar borrowed or contributed by shareholders to acquire those things.

## Details
The report adheres strictly to the fundamental accounting equation where assets equal liabilities plus equity. It is divided into current items expected to turn into cash or be settled within one operating cycle or twelve months, and non-current items held for long-term production. Analysts review working balances to judge solvency and capital allocation.

## Technical definition
A point-in-time financial statement reporting cumulative economic resources controlled by an entity and the simultaneous legal and residual claims against those resources.

## Examples
A manufacturing firm reports $50 million in property and cash, balanced against $30 million in bank loans and vendor payables plus $20 million in contributed capital and retained earnings.

## Easy explanation
A bank transfer works like sending an email with digital cash attached: instead of carrying paper banknotes across town, your bank deducts the sum from your account and instructs the receiver's bank to credit their balance.

## Details
Transfers move through central interbank clearing systems such as Fedwire and CHIPS for high-value real-time gross settlement, the Automated Clearing House (ACH) for retail batch processing, or instant networks like FedNow and SEPA Instant. To initiate a transfer, the sender provides the recipient's name, account number, and bank routing code (such as an ABA routing number or IBAN). Processing times range from instant settlement within seconds to several business days for standard international wires, which rely on the SWIFT messaging network.

## Technical definition
An electronic debit-credit instruction executed across depository institutions to shift central bank reserve balances or commercial bank liabilities from an originating account to a beneficiary account.

## Examples
A small business owner initiates a $4,500 supplier payment through online banking, routing funds directly from her commercial checking account to the vendor's account via the national automated clearing network.

## Easy explanation
Instead of adjusting your recipe after tasting a single spoonful or waiting until an entire banquet is served, you taste a bowl of four spoonfuls combined and adjust your seasoning based on that average.

## Details
Batch size directly balances hardware utilization against gradient noise. Full-batch gradient descent processes all records at once, requiring vast memory. Stochastic gradient descent computes gradients per single sample, introducing severe noise. Modern practice utilizes mini-batches (e.g., 32, 64, 256) loaded into accelerator memory, achieving parallel matrix multiplication throughput while maintaining sufficient stochastic regularization for generalization.

## Technical definition
The cardinality of the subset of training instances evaluated concurrently to compute an average empirical loss gradient for a single parameter update step.

## Examples
Setting the batch size to 128 images during vision training so that activations consume 14 GB of GPU memory without exceeding hardware capacity.

## Easy explanation
Unlike classic Bluetooth designed for continuous audio streaming that drains phone battery within hours, Bluetooth Low Energy stays asleep almost all the time, waking up for just a fraction of a millisecond to send quick sensor readings before sleeping again.

## Details
BLE operates in the globally unlicensed 2.4 GHz ISM band, dividing spectrum into 40 RF channels (3 channels reserved for discovery advertising and 37 for bidirectional data transfers). Its client-server data hierarchy is governed by the Generic Attribute Profile (GATT), structuring payload data into Services and readable/writable Characteristics identified by UUIDs. Because duty cycles are kept under one percent, small sensors and wearable peripherals can operate reliably for multiple years on a standard CR2032 coin cell.

## Technical definition
A wireless personal area network standard managed by the Bluetooth SIG designed to provide novel low-power, short-range radio communication for battery-constrained peripheral devices.

## Examples
A continuous glucose monitor worn on an arm that periodically transmits real-time blood sugar telemetry to a nearby smartphone app via BLE GATT notifications.

## Easy explanation
A blockchain is like a shared digital notebook that hundreds of people keep identical copies of: whenever someone writes down a verified payment, every person updates their copy at the same time, making it impossible for any single individual to secretly erase or fake an entry.

## Details
A blockchain groups validated transaction data into sequential structures called blocks. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the preceding block, a timestamp, and a Merkle tree of recent transactions. This chaining structure creates an immutable historical audit trail, because modifying any historical record requires recalculating every subsequent hash across the network. Nodes achieve synchronization and reject double-spending attacks through distributed consensus protocols (such as Proof of Work or Proof of Stake). Blockchains can also execute self-enforcing smart contracts directly on-chain without intermediaries.

## Technical definition
A distributed database maintaining an append-only sequence of cryptographically linked data blocks validated through a decentralized consensus mechanism across independent network peers.

## Examples
The Bitcoin network records peer-to-peer monetary transfers across thousands of global validating nodes, minting a new block roughly every ten minutes that references the cryptographic header of the prior block.

## Easy explanation
Picture a theater with two identical stages next to each other: while the actors perform on Stage Blue, the crew sets up Stage Green behind the curtain. At intermission, the spotlight swings instantly to Stage Green.

## Details
In a blue-green strategy, one environment (e.g., Blue) serves live user traffic while the duplicate environment (Green) hosts the newly deployed version. Engineers execute smoke tests and verification against Green in isolation. Once approved, the router or load balancer switches incoming traffic from Blue to Green simultaneously, providing instant cutover and an immediate fallback path if needed.

## Technical definition
A deployment pattern maintaining parallel identical infrastructure stacks, transitioning active routing target bindings atomically between environments.

## Examples
A banking portal runs on the Blue cluster while version 3.0 is deployed and tested on Green; the load balancer routes all new incoming connections to Green at midnight.

## Easy explanation
Buying a bond is like acting as the bank: you lend money to a government or corporation, they pay you regular interest payments as a thank-you fee, and when the loan term ends, they return your original principal.

## Details
When governments or corporations need funding for capital projects, they issue bonds with specified par values, coupon rates, and maturity dates. In secondary markets, bond prices fluctuate inversely with benchmark interest rates: when prevailing market rates rise, existing lower-yielding bonds trade at a discount; when rates fall, existing higher-paying bonds trade at a premium. Unlike equity holders, bondholders hold senior creditor claims during corporate insolvency and bankruptcy restructuring.

## Technical definition
A contractual negotiable debt obligation under which an issuer promises to disburse periodic coupon payments and redeem the par principal amount at a fixed terminal date.

## Examples
An investor buys a 10-year Treasury note with a $10,000 par value and a 4.0% coupon rate, collecting $400 annually in interest before receiving the $10,000 principal repayment at maturity.

## Easy explanation
Yield is the real-world mileage you get from your investment: while the bond coupon is the manufacturer's nominal rating, your actual yield depends on how much you paid for the bond in the secondary market.

## Details
An investor purchasing a bond at par ($1,000) with a 5% coupon earns a 5% yield. However, if market interest rates rise and the bond's price falls to $950 (discount), the new purchaser earns a higher yield because the fixed $50 annual coupon represents a larger percentage of the $950 outlay, plus capital appreciation at maturity. Key metrics include current yield (annual dollar coupon divided by market price) and yield to maturity (YTM), which solves for the internal rate of return assuming all future coupon payments are reinvested at the same rate until maturity.

## Technical definition
The annualized internal rate of return equating the present discounted value of all future contractual bond cash flows (coupons and par redemption) to its current market price.

## Examples
A bond with a $1,000 face value and a 6% annual coupon ($60) trades at a discounted price of $920; its current yield equals approximately 6.52% ($60 / $920).

## Easy explanation
Imagine a shopper who opens the front door of a bookshop, glances briefly at the front desk for five seconds, turns right around, and walks straight back out onto the street without touching a single book.

## Details
Bounce rate historically quantified single-page sessions where a user entered and departed without triggering a secondary hit. In Google Analytics 4 (GA4), bounce rate represents the exact mathematical complement of engagement rate: the proportion of visits falling outside engaged thresholds (specifically visits shorter than 10 seconds, logging under two page views, or generating no conversion milestones). A high bounce rate on multi-step conversion funnels, checkout portals, or landing pages indicates critical friction, misleading ad promises, slow page loading, or poor device compatibility. Conversely, on informational articles or customer support lookup pages, a rapid exit may simply mean the visitor immediately found the exact phone number or answer they sought.

## Technical definition
The proportion of recorded web traffic sessions classified as unengaged, calculated in modern digital analytics as one hundred percent minus the measured engagement rate.

## Examples
An online appliance repair service launches a PPC campaign targeting emergency fixes; forty out of one hundred landing page visitors immediately press the back button within three seconds, registering a bounce rate of 40%.

## Easy explanation
Changing the shape of wall electrical sockets from flat pins to round pins, meaning existing plug cords cannot plug in without buying a new adapter.

## Details
Breaking changes occur when function parameters are removed, endpoint URL routes change, serialization payloads alter, or behavioral expectations shift. When a library publishes a breaking change, downstream applications cannot upgrade without modifying their code or failing compilation. In SemVer, breaking changes mandate an increment of the MAJOR version number.

## Technical definition
A modification to a programmatic interface or operational contract that invalidates assumptions of existing consumers, resulting in compilation failures or runtime anomalies.

## Examples
Renaming the public method `getUserData()` to `fetchUserProfile()` without a backward-compatible alias causes compile errors for all calling applications.

## Easy explanation
Breaking news is like a fire alarm going off in the newsroom: regular programming stops immediately to report a major event unfolding right now.

## Details
When significant events occur, wire services and news organizations publish short initial dispatches labeled breaking news. As reporters gather confirmed facts from authorities, these preliminary alerts expand into detailed rolling coverage with live blogs and field broadcasts. Editorial teams must resist speculation and verify eyewitness accounts to prevent errors while competing against social media rumors.

## Technical definition
Unscheduled journalistic reporting of newly emerging, urgent events that interrupts scheduled broadcast programming or website content layouts.

## Examples
Television networks cut away from afternoon shows to broadcast live helicopter footage of a passenger aircraft executing a safe emergency landing.

## Easy explanation
Like packing a travel suitcase with a strict weight limit, a budget assigns every dollar of your paycheck a designated pocket before you travel through the month, preventing costly overages.

## Details
Creating a budget starts with totaling take-home income and subtracting essential fixed obligations like rent, loan payments, and utilities. Discretionary spending for entertainment and dining out receives an intentional ceiling. Surpluses are channeled directly into emergency reserves or retirement investments. Modern budgeters often utilize envelope budgeting, zero-based allocation, or automated mobile applications to reconcile actual receipts against planned targets.

## Technical definition
A quantitative schedule of expected financial inflows and projected resource expenditures over a discrete future operating interval, utilized to manage liquidity and maintain personal solvency.

## Examples
A household earning $4,000 net monthly allocates $2,000 to fixed housing and groceries, $800 to discretionary leisure, and transfers the remaining $1,200 to debt reduction and high-yield savings.

## Easy explanation
Picture a countdown fuel gauge on an airplane flight: as flight hours tick away, the fuel meter should steadily descend toward zero right as the aircraft lands smoothly on the runway.

## Details
A burndown chart features time across the horizontal X-axis (days in a sprint) and outstanding work across the vertical Y-axis (story points or task hours). An "ideal line" slopes downward from the total initial commitment to zero at the sprint's conclusion. The "actual line" tracks genuine completion daily. When the actual line hovers above the ideal slope, the team is behind schedule and may need to renegotiate scope; when it dips below, work is running ahead of plan.

## Technical definition
A project tracking graphic that plots outstanding backlog effort as a function of elapsed time within a defined development iteration or release milestone.

## Examples
A team viewing their Day 7 burndown observes 25 story points remaining out of 30 committed, highlighting that blocked code reviews are preventing tasks from reaching the Definition of Done.

## Easy explanation
A byline is like an artist's signature in the corner of a painting: it clearly tells the audience whose reporting and writing they are reading.

## Details
The byline provides accountability and public transparency, attributing the reporting, writing, and analysis to designated journalists. It typically appears right below the headline or at the conclusion of the article, often accompanied by the writer's beat, email, or social handle. When several reporters collaborate across regions, publications use joint bylines or add contributing reporting credits at the article base.

## Technical definition
An attribution line displayed alongside a journalistic story naming the specific writer or field reporter who authored the work.

## Examples
Below the headline, the text "By Maria Nguyen in Geneva" informs readers that the Swiss diplomatic talks were covered by an eyewitness correspondent on site.

## Easy explanation
Keeping a cheat sheet of frequently dialed phone numbers right on your desk instead of looking them up in the heavy telephone directory every time.

## Details
Caches operate close to consuming components in memory (such as RAM or Redis). When a request arrives, the system checks for a cache hit; if absent (a cache miss), it fetches the canonical record from persistent disks, delivers it, and stores a copy with an expiration time-to-live (TTL).

## Technical definition
An intermediate, low-latency computational storage tier holding replicated copies of primary data to optimize read throughput and minimize access latency.

## Examples
Storing product catalog listings in an in-memory Redis key-value store to handle flash-sale traffic spikes without crashing the main SQL database.

## Easy explanation
When a street vendor finishes demonstrating a vegetable peeler, looks at the gathered crowd, and says "Step forward right now to take home your set at half price", that clear command is a call to action.

## Details
In conversion optimization, a call to action provides the vital link between audience attention and tangible commercial follow-through. Without explicit instruction, users frequently absorb marketing content passively without knowing what action to execute next. CTAs take varied digital forms: clickable interactive buttons on landing pages, text links within email newsletters, verbal prompts at the close of promotional videos, or banner overlays in video ads. Effective CTAs emphasize clarity, urgency, and compelling value exchange (such as "Start your free 14-day trial" or "Claim your discount") rather than ambiguous generic instructions. Visual contrast, whitespace, and strategic above-the-fold placement further enhance click responsiveness.

## Technical definition
A stimulus element within a marketing communication or user interface designed to elicit a discrete, immediate transactional conversion or navigational response from the recipient.

## Examples
A mobile fitness application displays a high-contrast coral button reading "Start 7-Day Free Trial" at the bottom of its onboarding screen, prompting new downloaders to set up their workout profiles.

## Easy explanation
Like coal miners carrying a canary into a mine shaft: if the sensitive bird detected dangerous gases early, the miners evacuated safely before anyone was harmed.

## Details
A canary deployment directs a tiny portion of user requests (such as 2% or 5%) to a fleet subset running the updated code. Telemetry systems closely observe error logs, latency spikes, and resource saturation against the baseline version. If all metrics remain healthy, traffic routing increases incrementally until 100% of workloads run on the new version.

## Technical definition
A progressive traffic-splitting deployment pattern that routes a controlled percentage of live inbound requests to an experimental release cohort.

## Examples
A video streaming service directs 1% of live connections to a newly compiled player version for twenty minutes, confirming no playback crashes before ramping up.

## Easy explanation
This statement tracks actual bank balance movements over time, showing where cash physically entered the business register and where cash was disbursed.

## Details
Because accounting income utilizes accruals, cash flow statements strip non-cash expenses like depreciation to reconcile balance sheet shifts. Cash movements are categorized into operations representing core business revenue, investing representing machinery or acquisitions, and financing representing loans, stock sales, and dividend distributions.

## Technical definition
A liquidity-centric financial report detailing net cash generated or consumed across standardized operating, investing, and capital-raising activities.

## Examples
A logistics business registers $5 million in net income but generates $8 million in operating cash because $3 million in depreciation required zero cash outflow this quarter.

## Easy explanation
Like a chain of local convenience stores: instead of ordering milk directly from a dairy farm 500 miles away every morning, you pick up a carton delivered in advance to the store around the corner.

## Details
CDNs deploy edge servers (points of presence, or PoPs) globally. When a user requests assets (such as images, video clips, CSS, or JavaScript), DNS routes them to the nearest edge location. If cached, the asset returns in milliseconds; if not, the CDN fetches it from the origin server, caches it locally, and serves the user.

## Technical definition
A globally distributed overlay network of caching edge nodes optimizing asset delivery via geo-DNS routing, TLS termination, and origin shielding.

## Examples
A news website hosted on servers in Singapore caches high-resolution breaking news photographs on CDN edge locations in Hanoi, Tokyo, and London.

## Easy explanation
Like a maths teacher who insists on seeing the working: writing out the steps catches mistakes a quick guess would make.

## Details
Asking for reasoning step by step, or giving examples that include reasoning, often improves accuracy on arithmetic, logic and multi-step questions. The visible steps also let people check the result. The method spends more output tokens, and the written explanation is not guaranteed to be the path the model actually took.

## Technical definition
A prompt engineering technique that elicits explicit intermediate reasoning steps from a large language model before its final answer.

## Examples
“A phone costs 8 million đồng with 15% off, then 10% VAT. What is the final price? Think step by step.” The model works out 6.8 million, then 7.48 million.

Think of churn rate as water leaking out of a bucket with holes: even if you keep pumping fresh water in from the top through marketing, you can never fill the bucket unless you patch the leaks causing existing customers to slip away.

## Details
Churn rate is a vital health metric for subscription and software-as-a-service (SaaS) businesses. It is calculated by dividing the number of customers lost during a period by the total customer count at the start of that period, expressed as a percentage. High churn indicates product friction, declining customer satisfaction, or intense competitive substitution. Product teams distinguish between voluntary churn (users deliberately canceling) and involuntary churn (payment card processing failures).

## Technical definition
The proportion of contractual subscribers or active users who discontinue their commercial engagement or subscription with a provider over a designated reporting interval.

## Examples
A cloud storage platform with 10,000 subscribers on the first day of the month loses 300 paying accounts by month-end, reflecting a monthly churn rate of (300 / 10,000) = 3%.

Picture a modern automobile factory: whenever a mechanic installs a newly designed component, robotic testers verify fitment instantly and prep the vehicle for delivery without manual bottlenecks.

## Details
Continuous integration encourages developers to merge their feature branches into a shared main branch frequently. Every push triggers an automated build runner that executes linters and test suites. Continuous delivery subsequently packages verified artifacts for staged environments, while continuous deployment automates the final release to production systems without human gatekeeping.

## Technical definition
An automated operational framework that couples version control events to sequential build, automated test, containerization, and rollout procedures.

## Examples
A backend developer commits a bugfix to Git; within four minutes, automated integration tests pass, creating a container artifact that deploys to the staging cluster immediately.

## Easy explanation
Think of an airport baggage handling system: luggage moves down a conveyor through x-ray scanning, weight inspection, sorting, and aircraft loading in strict linear order.

## Details
A CI pipeline organizes engineering tasks into structured phases such as build, unit test, security scan, and artifact publishing. Tasks within a phase can run in parallel across distributed workers to shorten feedback loops. If any job encounters a failure or test regression, execution stops immediately, notifying the author.

## Technical definition
A directed execution graph declaring sequential stages and dependencies to validate source code and generate verified deployment artifacts.

## Examples
A GitHub Actions workflow where step one lints TypeScript code, step two executes parallel unit tests in 45 seconds, and step three uploads a production bundle.

## Easy explanation
Just like an electrical fuse box in your home: when a circuit overheats or shorts, the switch trips immediately to cut the current and prevent an electrical fire in the walls.

## Details
When remote services fail or experience high latency, calling threads accumulate waiting for timeouts, exhausting thread pools and triggering cascading system-wide crashes. A circuit breaker tracks failures within a sliding time window. In the Closed state, calls pass normally. When failure rates cross a configured threshold (such as 50% errors), it transitions to Open, immediately failing future calls with fallback responses. After a reset timeout, it enters Half-Open, allowing a trial batch of requests through to verify recovery.

## Technical definition
A fault-tolerance state machine wrapping remote operations to monitor failure frequencies, enforce rapid shedding of unhealthy dependencies, and facilitate graceful degradation.

## Examples
A checkout service encountering a 60% timeout rate on a third-party shipping quotation API trips its circuit breaker to open, immediately displaying cached flat rates to 800 waiting shoppers.

## Easy explanation
Like an onion with distinct protective layers: the delicate core in the center is the pure business idea, while outer layers handle cooking pans and seasonings that can be swapped without changing the core.

## Details
Formulated by Robert C. Martin, Clean Architecture organizes code into concentric rings: Entities at the center, surrounded by Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks and Drivers at the outer edge. The fundamental Dependency Rule mandates that code dependencies must only point inward toward higher-level policies. Inner business logic has zero dependencies on databases, UI frameworks, or third-party SDKs; instead, outer layers implement abstractions declared by inner layers using dependency inversion.

## Technical definition
A domain-centric architectural pattern enforcing strict inward directional dependency flow, ensuring business logic remains independent of persistence mechanisms and delivery mechanisms.

## Examples
A banking application where loan calculation rules reside in an inner entity layer, allowing engineers to replace the outer database engine from PostgreSQL to MongoDB without modifying a single line of financial calculation code.

## Easy explanation
CoAP is essentially a stripped-down, ultra-compact version of HTTP designed for tiny microchips: it lets small devices use familiar commands like GET and POST to request or send data over short UDP radio packets instead of heavy TCP streams.

## Details
Specified in RFC 7252, CoAP translates the familiar REST architectural model (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) into a binary-encoded protocol riding on UDP rather than TCP. It incorporates a compact four-byte fixed header and uses message identifiers to handle packet duplication and reordering. Reliability is provided at the application layer through confirmable (CON) messages requiring acknowledgment, or non-confirmable (NON) fire-and-forget packets. CoAP also supports native resource observation (RFC 7641) and blockwise transfers (RFC 7959) for larger payloads, secured natively by DTLS.

## Technical definition
An IETF standard application-layer web transfer protocol based on the REST model, optimized for constrained nodes and lossy networks through binary header encoding over UDP.

## Examples
A battery-powered parking space occupancy sensor transmitting a CoAP PUT request containing spot vacancy status to a municipal traffic server.

## Easy explanation
Having a fellow journalist proofread your investigative article before publication to ensure facts are solid and sentences are clear.

## Details
Code reviews are an essential step in modern continuous integration workflows. Team members inspect line-by-line diffs, evaluate edge cases, verify security practices, and suggest architectural simplifications. Besides catching flaws early, the process spreads domain expertise and establishes shared responsibility across the entire development team.

## Technical definition
A disciplined software quality assurance protocol where peers inspect proposed modifications against architectural guidelines, defect patterns, and stylistic requirements prior to upstream integration.

## Examples
A teammate reviews a pull request and points out that a newly added database query lacks pagination, preventing potential server timeouts.

## Easy explanation
Color grading is like putting mood lighting on a movie scene: warm golden hues make a summer memory feel nostalgic, while cold cyan tones turn a city street into a tense thriller.

## Details
Post-production workflows separate technical color correction (neutralizing color casts and matching exposure across clips) from creative color grading. Colorists use dedicated grading suites to sculpt lift, gamma, gain, and hue curves. Working in color-managed environments like ACES with wide dynamic range RAW footage, artists apply custom palettes, film grain emulations, and selective masks to direct viewer attention toward focal points.

## Technical definition
The creative post-production phase of altering luminance, chrominance, and color balance to achieve deliberate aesthetic atmospheres, narrative stylization, or brand palettes.

## Examples
A feature film colorist pushes shadows into deep teal and highlights into warm orange tones to give an action sequence a stylized, cinematic blockbuster visual appearance.

## Easy explanation
Like a rolling snowball: as it tumbles down the hill, it picks up snow faster and faster because it keeps getting bigger.

## Details
Every compounding period, accrued interest is added to the principal balance. Subsequent calculations determine interest from the enlarged sum, resulting in exponential growth over time.

## Technical definition
The addition of interest to the principal sum of a loan or deposit, so that the added interest also earns interest from that point forward.

## Examples
Investing $10,000 at 7% annual compounding produces:
- Year 1: $10,700
- Year 2: $11,449 (an extra $49 from interest on interest)
- Year 10: $19,671.51

## Easy explanation
Like placing numbered mailboxes around a circular running track: when a letter arrives with a number, you walk forward clockwise until you reach the nearest mailbox; adding a new mailbox only takes mail from its immediate neighbor.

## Details
Traditional hashing calculates node assignment using modulo arithmetic (hash(key) % N). When the node count N changes, nearly 100% of keys remap to new locations, obliterating cache hit ratios and triggering database stampedes. Consistent hashing maps both storage nodes and data keys onto a circular identifier ring (typically 0 to 2^32-1) using consistent hash functions like SHA-1. A key is stored on the first node encountered clockwise. When a node joins or leaves, only K/N keys move on average. Virtual nodes assign multiple random points to each physical server, ensuring smooth load balancing.

## Technical definition
A distributed partitioning scheme where keys and target nodes map onto a uniform circular identifier space, bounding data migration to a fraction of total items upon topological changes.

## Examples
A distributed caching cluster of 8 Memcached servers using consistent hashing where adding a 9th server causes only 11% of cached keys to be reallocated, leaving 89% of cache entries intact.

## Easy explanation
Think of a recipe in a cookbook or a master rubber stamp: the recipe itself never changes, but you can use it to bake dozens of identical cakes whenever you wish.

## Details
Container images consist of stacked, immutable filesystem layers created by build instructions (such as lines in a Dockerfile). Each layer captures file modifications or installed binaries. Because layers are content-addressed and shared across images on disk, pulling updated images requires downloading only newly altered layers.

## Technical definition
A standardized, serialized filesystem bundle combining content-addressed read-only layers with configuration JSON defining entrypoints and environment defaults.

## Examples
An image tagged `node:20-alpine` that packages a minimalist Linux root filesystem alongside the Node.js runtime, weighing approximately 50 MB.

## Easy explanation
Instead of constantly interrupting people with sales flyers, a gardening tools company publishes a free monthly illustrated guide on how to grow sweet tomatoes at home, so gardeners naturally think of that brand whenever they need new pruning shears.

## Details
Content marketing shifts organizational focus from overt transactional pitching to delivering genuine informational and educational value. Assets encompass blog essays, video walkthroughs, podcast episodes, downloadable industry research, and interactive templates. Rather than relying entirely on recurring paid advertising budgets, authoritative content assets compound in organic reach over time, earning backlinks, brand recall, and inbound search ranking. Search engines like Google prioritize helpful, reliable, people-first content written for human readers rather than manipulative search engine optimization formulas. By consistently answering consumer queries and solving domain challenges, brands nurture long-term customer loyalty and establish category thought leadership.

## Technical definition
A strategic marketing management methodology centered on the planned ideation, production, curation, and syndication of editorial media assets engineered to satisfy user intent and cultivate commercially profitable customer engagement.

## Examples
A cloud database provider creates an in-depth video tutorial series comparing distributed SQL database architectures, attracting three hundred thousand software engineers and establishing the company as the premier authority in database engineering.

## Easy explanation
If prompt engineering is writing a clear memo to an executive, context engineering is designing their entire briefing folder: ordering the reports, summarizing attachments, weeding out duplicate emails, and highlighting key data so they make decisions without information overload.

## Details
As context windows expanded from thousands to millions of tokens, simple prompt wording gave way to broader context engineering. The discipline involves strategically organizing system rules, dynamic few-shot examples, tool schemas, conversation histories, retrieved documents, and cached artifacts. It addresses failure modes like "lost-in-the-middle" attention degradation, context truncation, latency spikes, and token costs by employing compaction, pruning, and structured markup.

## Technical definition
The architectural discipline of designing, orchestrating, and optimizing the tokenized information payload presented to language models to maximize reasoning quality while minimizing latency and cost.

## Examples
An engineering team structuring a large codebase context using hierarchical XML tags, cached system headers, and compact symbol summaries, reducing token usage by 60% while improving bug resolution rates.

## Easy explanation
Picture a desk of fixed size: the documents, the conversation and the answer being written must all fit on it, and when it is full something has to come off.

## Details
The window is counted in tokens, not words. Everything shares it: the system prompt, the history, attached files, tool results and the generated answer. Larger windows let the model use more material but take longer and cost more. When a chat outgrows the window, older parts have to be dropped or summarised.

## Technical definition
The token budget of one request: the largest combined amount of input and generated output that a model can handle at once.

## Examples
A window of 200,000 tokens holds a few hundred pages of text: enough for a long contract and questions about it, but not for a codebase of millions of lines.

## Easy explanation
If one hundred customers walk into a shoe store and three of them walk up to the cash register and purchase shoes, the store's conversion rate for that afternoon is exactly three percent.

## Details
Conversion rate measures how effectively commercial websites and landing pages turn inbound web traffic into tangible business value. A conversion can represent a macro-conversion (such as completing an e-commerce checkout, subscribing to a software plan, or requesting a commercial sales quote) or a micro-conversion (such as downloading an informational whitepaper or creating an account). Calculated mathematically by dividing total verified conversions by total site visits or clicks and multiplying by one hundred, conversion rate highlights user experience bottlenecks, checkout friction, and pricing mismatches. Conversion rate optimization (CRO) systematically tests copy, layout, and value propositions via A/B testing to lift this metric.

## Technical definition
A fundamental digital analytics effectiveness ratio computed as the total count of successfully executed goal events divided by the aggregate number of qualifying user sessions or ad clicks.

## Examples
An online coffee supplier logs 10,000 unique user sessions on its store over one week and records 250 successful checkout transactions, delivering an e-commerce conversion rate of 2.5%.

## Easy explanation
Like a coat-check ticket handed to you at a club: when you return to the counter, handing back the ticket proves which coat is yours.

## Details
Managed via HTTP headers (`Set-Cookie` and `Cookie`), cookies maintain persistent sessions, store preferences, and enable cross-site tracking when not restricted by SameSite flags.

## Technical definition
A localized data packet conforming to RFC 6265 exchanged between a web server and client browser to enable state management over stateless HTTP.

## Examples
Preserving items inside an e-commerce shopping cart across page reloads.

## Easy explanation
Copyright is like a legal lock on your creative work: because you wrote the book or painted the canvas, nobody else can sell copies without your permission.

## Details
Copyright vests automatically the instant an original creative work becomes fixed in a tangible form, such as on paper, hard drive, or audio tape. Under international treaties like the Berne Convention, protection extends across borders without mandatory state registration. Copyright divides into economic rights (reproducing, performing, translating, and distributing for profit) and moral rights (the enduring right to be credited and prevent derogatory mutilation).

## Technical definition
A legal framework granting creators exclusive statutory monopolies over the reproduction, distribution, public performance, and adaptation of original literary, musical, and artistic works.

## Examples
A novelist retains copyright over their manuscript, granting a publisher exclusive rights to print paperbacks while licensing separate rights to a film studio for a cinematic adaptation.

## Easy explanation
Like an embassy visa check: when visitors from country A want to enter country B, border officials inspect country B's declared entry rules before stamping their passports.

## Details
By default, browsers enforce the same-origin policy, blocking scripts from requesting resources from a different domain, protocol, or port. CORS relaxes this policy securely by utilizing HTTP response headers such as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and preflight `OPTIONS` requests to approve cross-domain transfers.

## Technical definition
A browser enforcement protocol using dedicated HTTP request and response headers to grant cross-origin access permissions beyond the same-origin security boundary.

## Examples
A frontend hosted at `https://shop.example.com` reading inventory figures from an API hosted at `https://api.example.com` after verifying the returned origin permission header.

## Easy explanation
Think of a store that only pays the delivery courier when a customer actually opens the door and takes the package inside, rather than paying just to have the delivery van drive past the house.

## Details
Cost per click is the standard commercial billing framework for search engine advertising platforms like Google Ads and Microsoft Advertising. Advertisers configure a maximum CPC bid representing the highest price they are willing to pay for an individual visitor. During real-time auctions, the actual CPC billed is typically determined through second-price auction dynamics combined with quality score weighting, meaning an advertiser frequently pays just enough to beat the next highest competing ad rank.

## Technical definition
A pay-per-click billing settlement mechanism and unit economic metric determined by total advertising expenditure divided by the aggregate count of verified inbound click events.

## Examples
A dental clinic spends $500 on Google Search ads targeting emergency appointments and generates 100 clicks from prospective patients, resulting in an average cost per click of $5.

## Easy explanation
The CPI tracks the total price tag of an imaginary shopping cart containing everyday items like bread, electricity, rent, and bus fares to see how living costs change.

## Details
Statistical statistical bureaus collect thousands of retail quotes monthly, assigning relative weightings based on typical household consumption surveys. Comparing current basket totals against historic reference periods calculates the annualized headline rate of consumer inflation used for indexing pensions and collective labor contracts.

## Technical definition
A Laspeyres-type or chained weighted price index monitoring the temporal cost variations of a fixed representative basket of household consumption commodities.

## Examples
When the national CPI index climbs from 120.0 to 123.6 over twelve months, it documents an annual consumer inflation rate of 3.0 percent.

## Easy explanation
Think of renting space on a highway billboard: you pay a flat rental rate based on the estimated thousand cars that drive past each day, regardless of whether any driver stops to call the phone number on the sign.

## Details
Derived from the Latin word mille meaning thousand, CPM represents the traditional buying currency for display banners, programmatic video networks, and social media branding campaigns. Advertisers choose CPM when their primary objective is broad visibility and repeated brand exposure rather than direct transactional response. Ad servers track every valid ad render; once one thousand verified views accumulate, one unit of CPM cost is debited. Modern ad networks increasingly utilize viewable CPM (vCPM) to guarantee that at least fifty percent of the creative pixels remained in viewport for a minimum duration.

## Technical definition
A media buying valuation standard specifying the financial expenditure incurred for every 1,000 recorded ad rendering units across display, video, or social inventory.

## Examples
A soft drink brand launches a nationwide summer campaign buying 2,000,000 video banner impressions at a CPM of $6, incurring a total marketing placement budget of $12,000.

## Easy explanation
Like a restaurant kitchen: the order ticket written by the waiter goes straight to the cooking line to prepare the food, while the illustrated dining menu in the front room is designed exclusively for guests to browse dishes quickly.

## Details
In traditional software, a single domain model handles both writing state changes and serving complex query reads. This leads to contention, complex database joins, and unoptimized indexes. CQRS splits the application into two paths: Commands execute business rules, validate domain aggregates, and persist updates; Queries read denormalized, read-optimized projection stores (like Elasticsearch or Redis) without side effects. Changes synchronize asynchronously between write and read databases, enabling independent performance scaling for read-heavy workloads.

## Technical definition
An architectural design pattern segregating modification operations (Commands) from read operations (Queries), utilizing dedicated data schemas and execution pathways.

## Examples
An airline booking engine processing seat reservations on a relational write database with strict transactional locks, while projecting seat availability onto an in-memory cache answering 20,000 passenger flight searches per second.

## Easy explanation
Creative Commons is like a buffet menu for copyright: instead of saying "all rights reserved", creators mark their work with simple symbols telling everyone exactly how they can share or use it.

## Details
Creative Commons licenses sit on top of underlying copyright, allowing creators to retain ownership while granting advance public permissions. Licensors select from four core conditions: Attribution (BY), ShareAlike (SA), NonCommercial (NC), and NoDerivatives (ND). Combining these modular clauses yields six primary licenses, alongside CC0 for dedicating works to the public domain. Platforms like Wikipedia and open-access scientific journals rely heavily on these licenses to foster global collaboration.

## Technical definition
A suite of free, legally enforceable copyright licenses offering standardized permissions to copy, distribute, and remix intellectual works under human-readable and machine-readable metadata conditions.

## Examples
A photographer uploads landscape pictures under a CC BY-SA license, allowing bloggers to publish the images freely provided they credit the photographer and release derivative works under identical terms.

## Easy explanation
A credit card is like an ongoing, short-term tab at your local store: the issuing bank vouches for you and pays the merchant today, and at the end of the monthly billing cycle, you settle the total bill.

## Details
Unlike debit cards which draw immediately from deposit accounts, credit cards provide revolving unsecured credit. Issuers grant an interest-free grace period (typically 21 to 25 days) where no finance charge accrues if the full statement balance is paid on time. If a balance rolls over, compound interest applies at the card's annual percentage rate (APR), which often exceeds 20%. Cards also provide statutory consumer protections against unauthorized transactions, fraud liability caps, and promotional rewards such as cash back or travel points.

## Technical definition
A revolving credit facility linked to a physical or digital payment instrument, authorizing the cardholder to draw on an unsecured credit line up to a contractually determined limit.

## Examples
A consumer purchases a $900 laptop using a credit card on October 1st and repays the full $900 before the due date on November 20th, incurring zero interest while earning 2% cash back.

## Easy explanation
A credit score is like a school report card for borrowing money: if you turn in assignments on time and manage your workload responsibly, you get high marks that make lenders eager to trust you.

## Details
Credit bureaus compute this score using standardized models like FICO or VantageScore, typically ranging between 300 and 850. Major scoring components include payment history (35%), credit utilization ratio (30%), length of credit history (15%), credit mix (10%), and recent inquiries (10%). Higher scores unlock preferential terms, such as lower annual percentage rates (APR) on auto loans and mortgages, higher credit limits, and waiving security deposits on utilities.

## Technical definition
A statistically derived, standardized metric quantifying the probability that an obligor will experience a delinquency event or default on contractual credit obligations within a specified forecast horizon.

## Examples
Two people apply for the same 30-year mortgage. The one with a 780 score is typically offered a lower interest rate than the one with a 630 score, and across 30 years of repayments that gap can add up to tens of thousands of dollars in interest.

## Easy explanation
Crisis communication is like emergency dispatch during a storm: leaders must share clear, calm, and honest instructions so people stay safe and do not panic from rumors.

## Details
When organizations confront environmental disasters, product recalls, data breaches, or legal scandals, crisis communication protocols activate immediately. Specialists establish a centralized war room to gather facts, monitor social media sentiment, and coordinate public briefings. Best practices require swift acknowledgment of responsibility, empathetic concern for affected parties, and transparent descriptions of remediation steps rather than defensive denials.

## Technical definition
A specialized subfield of public relations dedicated to designing and executing strategic communications that mitigate organizational harm during acute operational crises.

## Examples
Following an airline computer outage that grounded thousands of flights, the corporate communications division issues hourly video updates explaining recovery progress and detailing automatic passenger refunds.

## Easy explanation
Cryptocurrency is digital money that exists entirely as computer code: instead of relying on a government or bank to print paper bills and track who owns what, a global computer network enforces mathematical rules so no one can spend money they do not have.

## Details
Unlike traditional fiat currencies issued by sovereign monetary authorities, cryptocurrencies operate on decentralized peer-to-peer networks secured by public-key cryptography. Users generate a private key to authorize outgoing transactions and a public address to receive incoming funds. New currency units are typically minted through protocol-defined economic incentives such as block validation rewards, often with a mathematically enforced issuance cap. While offering borderless censorship-resistant value transfer, cryptocurrencies experience high price volatility and present consumer protection challenges relating to irreversible transactions and custody loss.

## Technical definition
A digital medium of exchange operating on a distributed cryptographic ledger that regulates unit generation and verifies transactions using asymmetric cryptography without reliance on a central intermediary.

## Examples
Bitcoin (BTC) operates as a decentralized digital store of value with a hard-coded maximum supply of 21 million coins, whereas Ether (ETH) serves as the native currency powering computational gas transactions on the Ethereum blockchain.

## Easy explanation
Like an imposter slipping an unsigned withdrawal slip into your personal bank folder right as you hand the folder to a bank teller; the teller processes the slip believing it came from you.

## Details
Browsers automatically include authentication cookies with cross-site requests. If an application relies solely on ambient credentials without anti-CSRF tokens or `SameSite` cookie flags, visiting an attacker's website can trigger background POST requests that perform privileged actions on the victim's behalf.

## Technical definition
A web application vulnerability where a malicious origin exploits browser credential-forwarding behavior to submit forged HTTP requests under an authenticated user's credentials.

## Examples
Visiting a rogue web page containing a hidden form that submits a fund transfer request to `https://bank.com/transfer` using the victim's active session cookie.

## Easy explanation
If one hundred people walk past a billboard announcing a free concert and five of them actually tear off a flyer slip to take home, your response rate is five percent: that is exactly what CTR measures online.

## Details
CTR serves as an essential efficiency gauge across paid advertising, organic search, and email marketing. Calculated by dividing total recorded clicks by total ad impressions and multiplying by one hundred, CTR reflects how enticing, relevant, and compelling an offer appears to its intended audience. In ad networks like Google Ads, high click-through rates positively influence ad rank algorithms and lower effective cost-per-click, signaling to the platform that users find the advertisement valuable.

## Technical definition
A performance metric expressing the frequency with which an impression converts into an intentional user navigation event, calculated mathematically as total clicks divided by total served impressions.

## Examples
An e-commerce shoe retailer displays a banner ad that appears 10,000 times on sports blogs and receives 350 user clicks, yielding a click-through rate of 3.5%.

## Easy explanation
Think of customer lifetime value as the difference between a one-time tourist buying a single coffee and a neighborhood resident who stops by every morning for five years: the regular neighbor represents vastly higher total value to the café owner over time.

## Details
Customer lifetime value estimates the financial worth of a customer relationship. In subscription models, a foundational formula multiplies Average Revenue Per User (ARPU) by the gross margin, divided by the customer churn rate. Alternatively, it equals average purchase value multiplied by purchase frequency and average customer lifespan. Comparing CLV directly against Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) governs marketing efficiency: healthy software businesses maintain an LTV-to-CAC ratio of at least 3:1.

## Technical definition
A financial projection forecasting the net aggregate margin or revenue contributed by an individual customer account across the entirety of their commercial lifecycle with a firm.

## Examples
A streaming platform with an average monthly fee of $15, a 70% gross margin, and a monthly churn rate of 2% calculates customer lifetime value as ($15 × 0.70) / 0.02 = $525 per subscriber.

## Easy explanation
Like an international disease naming registry: instead of doctors calling the same illness by five different local names, they use one agreed code so medical teams worldwide know exactly what to treat.

## Details
CVE provides a unified naming convention managed by MITRE and the National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Each assigned identifier follows the format `CVE-YYYY-NNNN`, accompanied by severity scores (CVSS), affected software versions, and public patch bulletins.

## Technical definition
A system of standardized, publicly registered reference identifiers that provides a common taxonomy for known information security vulnerabilities and exposures.

## Examples
Referencing `CVE-2021-44228` when discussing and patching the infamous Log4j remote code execution vulnerability across enterprise clusters.

## Easy explanation
Think of DAU as the turnstile counter at the entrance of a public library: it registers each unique visitor who walks through the doors each day, counting each person only once regardless of how many books they check out.

## Details
Daily active users serves as a foundational measurement of user engagement and product growth. Crucially, tracking unique users rather than raw sessions or page views prevents heavy power users from artificially skewing activity totals. Teams must strictly define what constitutes an "active" interaction—such as sending a chat message or completing a transaction—rather than counting passive background app refreshes. Comparing DAU against Monthly Active Users (the DAU/MAU ratio) reveals product stickiness.

## Technical definition
A product analytics metric capturing the number of unique logged or verified individuals who complete at least one designated qualifying action within a calendar day.

## Examples
A social media platform logs 5 million DAU; if a user opens the mobile application twelve times throughout Monday, they are counted as exactly one unique daily active user.

## Easy explanation
Imagine a surgical team pausing for a brief sixty-second huddle before an operation to confirm patient details, verify instruments, and align roles so everyone moves with synchronized precision.

## Details
The Daily Scrum takes place at the same time and location every workday. It is designed specifically by and for the developers executing the sprint backlog. Traditionally framed around three questions—what was done yesterday, what will be addressed today, and what impediments exist—the meeting focuses squarely on progressing toward the sprint goal. Detailed architectural debates or side discussions are deferred to separate breakout sessions to keep the gathering concise.

## Technical definition
A timeboxed 15-minute event held each working day of a sprint in which the developers check how close they are to the sprint goal and adjust their plan for the remaining sprint backlog.

## Examples
At 9:30 AM, an engineering team gathers around their virtual board; one developer reports finishing API authentication, while another flags a blocking test environment issue requiring help.

## Easy explanation
Like a natural lake fed by multiple mountain streams: water flows in continuously and settles in its natural state until someone pumps it out for drinking, farming, or power.

## Details
Data lakes store data using inexpensive cloud object storage (such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage). Instead of requiring a predefined schema before writing (schema-on-write), they adopt schema-on-read, allowing data scientists to query raw files directly using tools like Trino or Spark.

## Technical definition
A centralized architecture allowing persistent retention of raw, untransformed data at any scale under a schema-on-read model.

## Examples
Storing terabytes of IoT sensor logs, social media video uploads, and raw database exports in an Amazon S3 bucket.

## Easy explanation
Like an automated municipal water system that draws water from a reservoir, passes it through purification and filtration plants, and pumps it reliably to kitchen taps.

## Details
Data pipelines can run in batch mode or real-time streaming mode using streaming brokers like Kafka. They handle schema validation, rate limiting, retry logic, and monitoring to ensure data flows reliably across disparate architectural components without human intervention.

## Technical definition
An end-to-end automated computational workflow encompassing the extraction, streaming or batch transport, transformation, and storage of digital data assets.

## Examples
Streaming user clickstream events through Apache Kafka, transforming them with Apache Flink, and writing the enriched records to Amazon S3.

## Easy explanation
Like a well-ordered department store warehouse where every box is barcode-labeled, cataloged, and placed on designated shelves for quick inventory audits.

## Details
Unlike transactional databases (OLTP) optimized for fast row writes, data warehouses (OLAP) use columnar storage, compression, and denormalized star schemas to execute complex aggregation queries over millions of historical records with minimal disk reads.

## Technical definition
